title: The lowest seat (Luke 14:1–14)
hookLine: don't take the top place; invite those who can't repay you

cards: A wedding reception, and no seating plan. Near the head table, a few empty chairs. At the back, by the kitchen door, a table where nobody seems to know anybody.

Where do you sit? Luke says Jesus is at a Sabbath dinner in the house of one of the chief Pharisees, watching the guests come in. He marks how they choose the chief rooms, the best places at the table.
And then, being Jesus, he says so.

teach.b: His advice starts out sounding like good manners. Don't grab the top place; someone more honored might arrive, the host will ask you to move, and you'll walk the whole room to the bottom with everyone watching.

Instead, in the King James Bible: "go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher." Room there means place, a seat at the table. This wasn't new wisdom.

The book of Proverbs says nearly the same: don't push yourself forward before the king, because it's better to be told come up here than to be put lower. Jesus is drawing on his own people's old wisdom.
Then he lifts it into something bigger: "For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted." That's not seating strategy anymore.
In Jesus' telling, it's how God turns things over. Then he turns to the host, and it gets more uncomfortable.
When you give a dinner, don't just invite friends, family and rich neighbors, who'll invite you back.
"But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee." He asks for a guest list of people who can't pay you back.
The repayment, he says, comes later, at the resurrection of the just. Lowest seat for the guest. Open door for the host.
Both are about letting go of the score.

how: Some churches and Christian groups run community meals and soup kitchens open to anyone, and some Christians make a habit of inviting people who are often left out to their own tables, especially at holidays.

games.q: you arrive at a grand dinner. there are empty places near the host and some at the back. where do you sit?
o: near the host. you were invited, after all.
you stand by the door until someone seats you.
games.why: "go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher."

practice: Run through the people you usually share meals or time with, and notice how many return the favor; that's normal and good.

Then widen the circle to someone who rarely gets invited anywhere, an older neighbor living alone, a new coworker, someone in a hard time with nothing to offer back, and picture setting a place for them at your table.
If you pray, ask for open doors.

wordCard.voice: Proverbs. The book Jesus echoes when he tells a dinner guest to take the lowest seat and let the host call him up higher, rather than pushing to the front.

orig.note: Greek: last, lowest. the lowest place at the table, the one Jesus tells the guest to take.

carryVoice: Your line: friend, go up higher. The host does the calling up, not the guest. That's day five hundred fifty-four.
